summary: Announces that the London node of the ARPANET has been connected since early September. It consists of a TIP and a local PDP-9 Host that front-ends the Rutherford High Energy Laboratory's IBM 360/195, linked to it by a 2.4 kbps line.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 588 announces that the London ARPANET node was up and describes its connection to Rutherford's IBM 360/195. Users could reach the system through a local PDP-9 for limited experimental work.

subtitle: An update on the London ARPANET node and its remote computing access.

tldr.problem: The RFC announces a London ARPANET node and explains how it connected users to a computer at Rutherford High Energy Laboratory.
tldr.mechanism: A local PDP-9 host front-ended the Rutherford IBM 360/195 over a 2.4 Kbps line; users connected to the PDP-9 and could log in to the 360 when a MAST port was available.
tldr.outcome: The 360 was available for limited experimental use, with a guest login restricted to demonstrations and a small CPU allowance.

today: RFC 588 is an announcement describing the London ARPANET node and the experimental access it offered to the Rutherford IBM 360/195.

sections.title: The London Node and Rutherford Connection
sections.content:
The London ARPANET node, address 42, had been connected since early September. It included a TIP at address 170 and a local PDP-9 host at address 0. That PDP-9 front-ended the Rutherford High Energy Laboratory's IBM 360/195, about 60 miles away, over a 2.4 Kbps line.

The RFC describes the PDP-9 as the first point of Telnet access. From there, a user could log in to the 360 if one of its two MAST ports was available, enter and edit files with ELECTRIC, submit them to the batch stream and inspect output interactively.
sections.plainLanguage: Users reached the London node's local PDP-9, which connected them to Rutherford's IBM 360/195. They could edit files, submit batch work and inspect the output when a MAST port was free.

sections.title: Available Use and Limits
sections.content: The RFC says the 360 was available for limited experimental use and provided a free GUEST login for demonstrations. That account allowed one minute of CPU time per week, and its jobs had to be Class X with a maximum run time of 10 seconds. It was not planned as a normal service host; cooperative projects involving a US group and an interested UK party were invited.
sections.plainLanguage: The 360 was available for experiments, not as a general service. Its free guest account was limited to demonstrations and had strict limits on CPU time and job duration.

sections.title: Protocols and Planned Facilities
sections.content:
The PDP-9 had IMP-HOST, HOST-HOST, ICP and Telnet protocols in place. The RFC says printing jobs at TIPs and implementing RJE and FTP were future plans, not current features. It also notes that other hosts were expected eventually to connect through the Very Distant Host Interface.

Help was available from the PDP-9 and the 360 through their stated commands. The RFC gives planned availability times and describes how users could contact the site about access or connection problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet access and interactive editing were available, while RJE, FTP and TIP job printing were still planned. The announcement also describes help and contact arrangements for users.
